passage: Mr Bhatia announced that the science fair groups had changed and each team would present tomorrow, not next week. A few students groaned. Pema kept her face blank, eyebrows level, and said, "Fantastic, I love surprises," and the row around her laughed. Inside, she had no idea which chart he meant by 'the variable sheet'. Varun caught her twisting her pen cap. At the library after last bell he slid into the seat beside her. "Can I check something? I didn't understand the variable sheet." Pema's shoulders dropped. "Me neither. I was pretending." They opened the sheet together, and by the time the librarian switched off the lights she had said each step aloud and written it down.

qa.q: When would the teams present according to Mr Bhatia?
qa.a: He said each team would present tomorrow, not next week.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling behind her joke about loving surprises?
qa.a: She was probably confused and a bit anxious, since she did not know what the variable sheet was and twisted her pen cap. The joke may also have simply been her way of fitting in with the class.

qa.q: What made Varun's approach work?
qa.a: He asked privately and admitted his own confusion first, so Pema could stop pretending without losing face.

qa.q: How might Varun have read Pema's blank face at the time?
qa.a: He may not have been sure whether she was calm or lost, which is why a quiet check afterwards made sense.

grounding: A teenager masks surprise and confusion with a poker face and a joke, and a private check sorts out understanding.

passage:
Dear Abhinav bhaiya,

You asked how my new section is going. Honestly, something small happened that I want to tell you. On Monday our teacher said the exam pattern would change and I felt my stomach drop. I kept my face flat and said, "Wow, nice," like it was nothing. Everyone was joking, so I joked too. I didn't understand what 'weighted marks' meant. All evening I kept thinking I'd look silly if I asked. Then I remembered what you told me last summer about asking privately. So I stayed back after class on Tuesday and asked Sir to explain it once more. He drew an example. It made sense.

Thanks for the advice. Write soon.

Yusuf 🙂

qa.q: What did the teacher announce on Monday?
qa.a: The teacher said the exam pattern would change.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf keep a flat face and say "Wow, nice"?
qa.a: Yusuf probably felt confused and worried about looking silly in front of classmates, so copied the joking mood. Perhaps Yusuf also did not want to slow the class down.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do next if a later change still feels unclear?
qa.a: Yusuf could go back to a teacher privately, as on Tuesday, or ask a trusted friend to walk through an example.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He may feel pleased that his advice helped, and glad Yusuf trusts him enough to share an embarrassing moment. 😊

grounding: A teenager hides confusion with a joke in front of peers and sorts it out with a private check afterward.

passage:
Kiran, you asked why I, Shalini, never put my hand up in physics. Okay, here's the honest version.
In the first week, Sir wrote this huge equation for momentum and said, "Simple, na?" Everyone nodded. I had no idea what it meant, like zero, but I just raised my eyebrows and said, "Wow, so easy, I could do it asleep." Big laugh. Sir laughed too.
And that's the trap, right? Once you've made the joke, you can't then say you're lost.
It was only when Sir kept me back two days later, in the empty lab, and asked, "Shalini, that joke on Monday, was it cover?" that I nodded. He went through it again with a ball and a bucket. Ten minutes. I finally got it.
So now, if I'm joking loudly in class, you're allowed to poke me.

qa.q: What did Shalini say after Sir called the equation simple?
qa.a: Shalini said, "Wow, so easy, I could do it asleep."

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling behind the joke, and how else could her classmates have read it?
qa.a: Shalini was confused and probably embarrassed to be the only one lost, so the joke hid it. Her classmates could easily have read it as real confidence or just her being funny.

qa.q: What could Kiran do if Shalini jokes loudly in class again?
qa.a: Kiran could check in quietly afterwards, away from the others, and ask if the joke was cover, the way Sir did in the empty lab.

qa.q: What was it like for Sir to hear a laugh instead of a question?
qa.a: From Sir's side the class seemed to understand, and only the private check two days later showed that the laugh had hidden confusion.

grounding: The monologue shows a teen masking confusion with a joke in front of peers and a private check revealing what had not been understood.

passage:
I sit next to Ujjwal in computer lab, so I saw it. When Ma'am announced we'd be coding in a new language from Monday, half the class groaned. Ujjwal didn't blink. Face like a wall. He just said, "Cool," and went on typing.
But his fingers had stopped. He was typing the same line, deleting it, typing it again. I can't read minds, so maybe he was only tired. Still, he usually jumps on anything new.
At lunch I didn't ask in front of the others. On the way to the bus I said, "That new language thing... did you get what she meant, or was it a surprise?"
He laughed. "Total surprise. I thought we'd finish the old one first. I didn't want to look lost."
We went through the first worksheet together on the bus.
- Ira

qa.q: When would the class start coding in the new language?
qa.a: The class would start coding in the new language from Monday.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have been feeling behind his poker face, and how can Ira tell?
qa.a: His face stayed blank and he said "Cool," but his fingers kept typing and deleting the same line, which hints he was surprised and a bit anxious. Ira admits he may just have been tired.

qa.q: What small step did Ira take that helped?
qa.a: Ira waited until they were alone on the way to the bus and asked gently, so Ujjwal could admit the surprise without looking lost in front of peers.

qa.q: What was it like for Ujjwal to keep a poker face while the class groaned?
qa.a: He probably felt pressure to look unbothered and quick, so he held back his surprise even though he was confused inside.

grounding: A classmate's account shows a teen hiding surprise with a poker face and a private check sorting out whether he understood.

passage:
Monday: At basketball practice, Coach Rao announced a new zone defence and drew arrows all over the board. Disha had never heard of a zone. She folded her arms, nodded slowly and said, "Obviously," which made the others grin.
Wednesday: In the drill, Disha kept drifting to the wrong corner. When Coach shouted her name, she threw up her hands and joked, "I was testing if you were awake!" Laughter again. But she bit her lip on the bench afterwards and did not drink her water.
Friday: Preeti waited until the rest had left the court. "Hey, the zone thing. Did Coach's drawing make sense to you? Because it didn't to me at first."
Disha let out a breath. "Not one arrow."
They walked it through with two water bottles as players. By Saturday's match, Disha was in the right corner every time.

qa.q: What did Disha say when Coach shouted her name on Wednesday?
qa.a: She threw up her hands and joked, "I was testing if you were awake!"

qa.q: What does Disha's lip-biting on the bench suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt worried and embarrassed about not understanding the zone, even though her jokes made her seem relaxed. She might also just have been annoyed with herself for a bad drill.

qa.q: Why did Preeti's approach on Friday work?
qa.a: Preeti waited until they were alone and admitted her own confusion first, which made it easy for Disha to say she hadn't understood without losing face.

qa.q: How might Coach Rao have seen Disha's jokes during the week?
qa.a: Coach might have read them as cheek or lack of focus, rather than as a cover for not understanding the new defence.

grounding: The before, during and after beats show a teenager masking surprise and confusion with a poker face and jokes, and a private check sorting it out.

passage: Sit, Sabina, and stop hiding that report card behind the cushion. Your Nani Urmila was no genius either. When I was in class nine, our maths teacher, Mrs D'Souza, drew a new sign on the board, a little sideways eight. Infinity, she said. The whole row gasped, and I had no idea why. So I did what I always did: I rolled my eyes and whispered, "Big deal, it's just a lazy eight," and my friend Rukmini laughed so hard she got scolded. Everyone thought I knew. I didn't. My face stayed blank all period, but inside I was spinning. That evening I went to Mrs D'Souza's quarters with a plate of my mother's laddoos as an excuse and said, "Ma'am, I didn't follow any of it." She laughed, sat me on her step and drew it again, slowly, until I did.

qa.q: What sign did Mrs D'Souza draw on the board?
qa.a: She drew a little sideways eight, which she said was infinity.

qa.q: What was young Urmila feeling behind the joke about a lazy eight?
qa.a: Urmila was confused and probably embarrassed to be the only one who didn't get it, and the eye-roll and joke masked that. It may also have been nervousness about looking slow in front of the row.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Urmila actually understand?
qa.a: Going to Mrs D'Souza privately that evening and admitting 'I didn't follow any of it' turned a hidden gap into a real lesson.

qa.q: How did Rukmini and the others read Urmila's joke?
qa.a: They took it as a sign that Urmila already knew; Rukmini laughed so hard she got scolded, so nobody guessed the confusion underneath.

grounding: It shows a teenager hiding confusion behind a joke and a blank face in front of classmates, then checking privately later to really understand.
